claim: Utility of a memory update = gain x need (gain: how much it would change the choice; need: expected near-term visits to the state). One rule yields forward replay before action and reverse replay after surprise. It is a model with fixed parameters, matched to published rat data only qualitatively.
agent_test: Rank stored subgoals by gain x need versus recency versus random at equal tokens on multi-step tasks.

claim: Gain, not need, carries the empirical signal. Reverse replay rose with reward size and fell with reward removal in rats; in humans learning from non-local paths was faster for high-gain paths (alpha 0.79 vs 0.37, p=0.020) but not high-need paths (0.61 vs 0.54, p=0.16).
agent_test: Order by gain only, need only, and product; expect gain-only to capture most of the benefit.

claim: Reverse replay is selective for reward change while forward replay is not (rats: reverse z=3.57 vs forward z=0.305; humans: 160 ms backward replay tracked utility, 30 ms forward replay did not, p=0.74).
agent_test: After a failure or changed fact, revisit upstream steps backward from the change point; compare with forward re-read at equal tokens.

claim: Offline reinstatement of old states predicts re-planning after a reward change, and only when revaluation is needed (rho 0.54 vs -0.13; difference p=0.023; N=24). Replay also fades across rests as prediction errors shrink.
agent_test: Trigger revisit of stored subgoals only when new evidence changes their value; skip otherwise; compare with always-revisit.

claim: Replay is causally useful: interrupting awake ripples impaired spatial learning, and replay re-routes around moved barriers. Read from abstracts only.
agent_test: Not testable on an agent; background only.

claim: Replay content does not reliably follow the upcoming choice. In rats it favoured the previous goal (about two-fold) and future-arm enrichment was small and not present in all animals. Carey 2019 (preprint full text read; 4 rats, 19 sessions) found replay content biased AWAY from the arm preferred that day (content vs choice r(19)=-.75, p<.001), even before the day's task. Gagne and Dayan 2022 show a gain-based model with forgetting can produce such pessimal replay, so the result limits need-only and recency rules more than it limits gain x need. Tirole 2026 preprint (3 decoded rats) also finds awake replay tracks behavioural state, not reward size, and sleep replay favours the most recent episode regardless of reward.
schema_part: memory (guard against assuming revisits are plan-relevant)
agent_test: Test whether revisiting the option the agent currently disfavours or the last failed subgoal helps more than lookahead on the next planned step; include a stale-belief condition.

claim: Replay is not limited to recent or frequent paths: remote, rare and never-travelled paths are replayed, including preplay of a seen but unvisited rewarded arm.
agent_test: Keep a quota for rarely visited or untried subgoals so need-ordering does not starve them; compare with pure need order.

claim: Forward replay outnumbered reverse in a pausing design (40% forward vs 26% reverse of 263 events; 48% vs 25% for events over 250 ms), so the clean before-forward/after-reverse split is design-dependent. Diba and Buzsaki 2007 counts (841/887 forward before a run, 395/464 reverse after) were confirmed in the Diba full text (author manuscript): 36% forward vs 19% reverse of significant events, 841/887 and 395/464.
agent_test: Do not hard-code direction; let gain and need decide.

claim: Prioritising replay by prediction error speeds deep RL: rank-based PER raised DQN median human-normalised score 48% to 106% on 49 Atari games and beat uniform replay on 41 of 49.
agent_test: Compare priority-by-error against uniform sampling of stored lessons at equal tokens.

claim: Raw error-based prioritisation is brittle: it was worse than uniform in several settings (SAC, Seaquest, SpaceInvaders), gave limited benefit in larger buffers without n-step returns, and a very large buffer slows learning. Panahi 2024 (abstract) finds no prioritised variant consistently beats uniform replay in control tasks with neural networks. Yoo 2026 adds that naive uniform or group-level replay in GRPO gave no consistent gain and fell 0.83 and 1.82 pp below no-replay at 4B.
agent_test: Always run a uniform-order control and report where priority loses.

claim: Stale priority is the failure mode in LLM RL: PER with priority=|reward| underperformed on-policy; exponential age decay fixed it (peak +46% NQ Search, +367% Sokoban Simple, +133% VLM FrozenLake, +18% AIME vs on-policy; little benefit on GSM8K). Best decay constant depends on policy drift (tau=500 on fast-drift Sokoban, 1000 on FrozenLake). DyJR finds a short recency window best (M=8: 34.1; M=64: 30.9).
agent_test: Weight stored subgoal value by age; test decay vs none when the problem state changed mid-episode.

claim: Ranking LLM rollouts by absolute advantage with age cap 10, replay ratio 0.5 and fresh data in every batch beats GRPO by +0.61, +0.60, +1.66 points at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B.
agent_test: Keep fresh derivations in context alongside replayed ones; compare with replay-only.

claim: Moderate-difficulty selection plus recent rollout reuse cut GRPO fine-tuning time by 23% to 62% at equal performance (6 model-dataset pairs).
agent_test: Training-time only; not usable by a scaffold-only agent.

claim: P2Value (probability x test pass rate) ranks failed programs for replay in fine-tuning. Its large gains are mostly distillation from a stronger model (GPT-Neo APPS-mixed pass 5.73 -> 42.12 after fine-tuning on GPT-4-turbo samples); self-fine-tuning gains are small (GPT-2 7.30 -> 8.12; GPT-Neo 5.73 -> 5.39, down). The text read has no ordering-versus-uniform ablation, so ordering is not separated from filtering.
agent_test: Do not use as evidence for ordering. Needs a priority-vs-uniform ablation at equal sample count.

claim: Replay that keeps diversity matters. DyJR (Qwen3-4B-Base, six math sets) raises GRPO 29.8 to 34.1 (3 runs each for main comparison) and separates admission from use: confidence admission +2.5 (policy-gradient replay) and +3.7 (JS regularisation) points; JS adds +1.5 over policy-gradient replay when admission is fixed (0.3 under perfect-only admission). Ablations are single-run. The advantage-replay work keeps fresh data to avoid collapse.
agent_test: Check whether ordering by gain collapses the set of revisited subgoals.

claim: In the original model need is computed from the successor representation, but gain requires knowing the policy effect before the backup, which the authors call unrealistic. An LLM agent needs a cheap proxy for gain. Evidence on proxies: the self-rated importance proxy (Generative Agents) is the default but is untested and did no better than recency in a retention study (LoCoMo F1 0.016 vs 0.017 at budget 32); a learned outcome Q-value ranked memories well (MemRL, r=0.861 with success, 21.5% to 88.1% by bin); a cheap strength + similarity + inhibition-of-return rule approaches Mattar and Daw in RL (abstract only).
agent_test: Compare self-rated gain and need against measured benefit of revisiting on held-out problems.

claim: No study was found that tests gain x need ordering in a language-model agent by name. Nearest: MemRL (2026) orders stored episodes by a learned Q-value and beats similarity-only retrieval (average CSR 0.798 vs 0.699 for RAG and 0.760 for MemP), but with no recency or random control at equal tokens and with a reward critic that needs repeated tasks. The rest of the LLM evidence is replay ordering in RL fine-tuning. Update: Yoo 2026 (equal-count uniform control, +0.39 avg and +3.39 pass for |advantage| ordering, training time), Chen and Cheng 2026 (recency 0.368 vs random 0.300 vs learned value 0.770 gold retention, retention not ordering) and WMT (event-refreshed scaffold memory, +9.97 pp over linear history, no recency or random control) are the nearest; still no prompt-time test of gain x need ordering against recency and random on revisit order.
agent_test: Run the first direct test of gain x need ordering of stored subgoals in a reasoning agent.

claim: Cheap-proxy ordering of agent memory: a learned outcome utility (Q-value mixed 50/50 with similarity) beat similarity-only RAG on four agent benchmarks, and the learned Q tracked success (r=0.861). It needs reward feedback over repeated tasks, so it is not a within-episode gain proxy, and the equal-token recency/random control is missing.
agent_test: Re-rank retrieved subgoals by a score updated from outcomes; compare with similarity-only, recency and random at the same number of items and tokens.

claim: Self-rated importance (LLM scores memory 1 to 10) is the common gain proxy but has no validation; in a budgeted retention test it matched recency (F1 0.016 vs 0.017 at budget 32; both below 0.03 at budget 128) while a mixed recency/question-overlap/learned score was 3 to 7 times better. Chen and Cheng 2026: a cue scored against the future question scores 0.979 only if it can see the question; blind it scores 0.286 (below random 0.300).
schema_part: memory (do not trust self-rated importance without a control)
agent_test: Measure rank correlation between self-rated gain and the measured change in answer quality after revisiting; drop the proxy if it does not beat recency.

claim: Priority staleness inside a learning run is costly and decay should track drift: FreshPER's best tau was 500 for fast drift and 1000 for slow drift; DyJR's best recency window was the shortest tested (M=8: 34.1 vs M=64: 30.9). No study measures decay inside a single reasoning episode with new evidence arriving. Update: WMT decays by missed selection (not elapsed time) and lets invalidation events suppress branches directly; MemDecay measured half-lives of 148 to 189 steps for system text vs 14 to 16 for scratchpad; a 2026 rat preprint also models priority as a decaying trace refreshed by remote replay. None ablates decay vs event reset.
agent_test: On new evidence, reset or discount priorities of items that depend on the changed fact; compare with a fixed time decay.

claim: Theory has extended Mattar and Daw for uncertainty (forgetting makes pessimal replay optimal; human MEG n=25, Spearman M=0.04, p=0.04) and for learned triggering (recurrent agent rollout probability vs human thinking time r=0.186, 94 participants), but no non-myopic multi-step replay value was found. Sagiv et al. 2025 (Neuron) extend the value to future as well as current goals (estimated chance of later relevance), a partial answer to the current-goal-only limit.
schema_part: memory (apply gain to chains, not single items)
agent_test: Score a subgoal together with its dependants before ordering; test against single-item scoring.

claim: Dyna-style agents guard against compounding model error by keeping simulated rollouts short and branched from real states (MBPO: k raised from 1 to 15 on Hopper; k=1 also worked). Prioritised error-based ordering can still spike errors with neural function approximators (Panahi 2024, abstract).
agent_test: Start any imagined continuation from a verified state; cap its depth; check it against real feedback.

claim: (Absence finding, search-limited) Gaps with no direct evidence after this search: replication of the human gain-over-need result (Liu 2021, N=29), reverse versus forward revisit in LLM multi-step tasks at equal tokens, and ordering by expected value of update versus recency and random at equal tokens. Update: a Neuron 2026 iEEG study (N=34, abstract only) extends the human prioritised non-local learning result (ripples carry which indirect experience is most valuable to update), so the Liu replication gap is now partial. Ordering-ablation gap partly closed by Yoo 2026 (training-time). Dependants-scored non-myopic gain and decay-vs-event ablations were searched for and not found.
agent_test: These are the three experiments worth running first.

claim: Backward replay at 160 ms in humans goes with faster non-local learning: learning rate 0.70 with significant replay vs 0.61 without (difference 0.09, p=0.023); the 30 ms forward replay gave a 0.01 difference. N=29, one task, no replication found.
agent_test: After a changed fact, compare backward re-derivation from the change point vs forward re-read at equal tokens on planted-error items.

claim: Naming the revisit target by the model's own first-error judgement beats a random revisit target in LLM reasoning RL at equal rollout count: SRPO best on 7/10 (14B) and 6/10 (7B) tasks, random reset about equal to GRPO; clean-prefix resets corrected 28.7% vs 16.3% Pass@4 for erroneous-region resets. This is training-time and tests where to revisit, not backward vs forward order.
agent_test: Compare 'revisit the step the model flags as first wrong' with a random step and with forward re-read at equal tokens on planted-error items.

claim: After a changed fact, stored beliefs fail mostly through dependants: on STALE (1,200 queries) the best plain model reached 55.2% overall, memory frameworks 5.1% to 17.8%, and a write-time dependency search (CUPMEM) 68.0%; propagated (Type II) conflicts were lower than direct ones in nearly all systems. No recency-vs-dependency ablation was reported.
agent_test: On a changed-fact task, revisit dependants of the changed item first vs recency-first at equal tokens.

claim: A scaffold that updates item scores by events, decays by missed selection, scores a whole branch (max plus mean minus failed and obsolete fractions) and suppresses on invalidation raised GAIA-Text accuracy +9.97 pp on average over linear history while using 32.8% fewer prompt tokens (3 small models, 127 questions, preprint). The ordering effect is not isolated and no recency or random control exists.
agent_test: Replicate the package in our harness and ablate each piece, including a recency-only and random-order control.

claim: Fixed-budget value ranking beats recency, and recency is close to random: keeping the top 30% of LongMemEval turns retained 0.770 of gold evidence with a learned value, 0.368 with recency and 0.300 at random. A relevance cue that peeks at the future question gets 0.979 but 0.286 when blind. This is retention, not revisit order.
agent_test: Never score need with information from the future question; test need cues that exist at decision time.

claim: Decay constants should differ by content type: measured half-lives were 148 to 189 decode steps for system text vs 14 to 16 for scratchpad reasoning (small models, KV cache), and rat sleep replay follows recency regardless of reward. Evidence is partial and from different levels (KV cache, rat replay).
agent_test: Use slow decay for plans and goals, fast decay for scratch notes, with event refresh; compare with one global decay.
